content: The antihypertensive effect of valsartan is achieved after four weeks of treatment. In long-term follow-up studies without placebo control, the effect of valsartan was sustained for up to two years. The blood pressure-lowering effect of valsartan is independent of age, gender, or race. However, the findings regarding race should be interpreted cautiously, as antihypertensive drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system (such as ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers) are generally less effective in individuals with low-renin hypertension (commonly observed in Black patients) compared to those with high-renin hypertension (commonly observed in White patients). In pooled, randomized, controlled trials of valsartan (Diovan) involving 140 Black patients and 830 White patients, valsartan and an ACE inhibitor control were found to be at least equally effective in Black patients as in White patients. The reason for this discrepancy from previous findings remains unclear. Abrupt discontinuation of valsartan has not been associated with a rapid increase in blood pressure. The blood pressure-lowering effects of valsartan and thiazide-type diuretics are approximately additive. Seven studies of valsartan monotherapy included over 2,000 patients randomized to various doses of valsartan and approximately 800 patients randomized to placebo. Doses below 80 mg were not consistently distinguishable from placebo at trough levels, but doses of 80 mg, 160 mg, and 320 mg produced dose-related reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure. The differences from placebo were approximately 6-9 mmHg systolic and 3-5 mmHg diastolic at doses of 80-160 mg, and 9 mmHg systolic and 6 mmHg diastolic at 320 mg. Patients with an inadequate response to 80 mg once daily were titrated to either 160 mg once daily or 80 mg twice daily, resulting in comparable responses in both groups. In controlled trials, the antihypertensive effect of valsartan 80 mg once daily was similar to that of enalapril 20 mg once daily or lisinopril 10 mg once daily. There are no trials of valsartan demonstrating reductions in cardiovascular risk in hypertensive patients, although at least one pharmacologically similar drug has shown such benefits. Valsartan-treated patients in controlled trials experienced essentially no change in heart rate. Pediatric Hypertension The antihypertensive effects of valsartan were evaluated in two randomized, double-blind clinical studies. In one study involving 261 hypertensive pediatric patients aged 6 to 16 years, those weighing less than 35 kg received daily doses of 10 mg, 40 mg, or 80 mg of valsartan (low, medium, and high doses), while those weighing 35 kg or more received daily doses of 20 mg, 80 mg, or 160 mg (low, medium, and high doses). The most common underlying causes of hypertension in these children were renal and urinary disorders, as well as essential hypertension with or without obesity. After two weeks of treatment, valsartan reduced both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in a dose-dependent manner. Overall, the three dose levels of valsartan (low, medium, and high) significantly reduced systolic blood pressure by -8 mmHg, -10 mmHg, and -12 mmHg from baseline, respectively. Patients were then re-randomized to either continue receiving the same dose of valsartan or switch to placebo. In patients who continued receiving medium and high doses of valsartan, systolic blood pressure at trough was -4 mmHg and -7 mmHg lower, respectively, than in those who received placebo. In patients receiving the low dose of valsartan, systolic blood pressure at trough was similar to that of patients who received placebo.
